source_text: ἐν μαθηταῖς, λέγων· «Κύριε, ἐπίτρεψόν μοι πρῶτον ἀπελθεῖν, καὶ θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου.» Ὁ δὲ, «Ἀκολούθει μοι, φησὶ, καὶ ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάπτειν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς·» νεκροὺς, οἶμαι, λέγων τοὺς τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ φρονεῖν ἑλομένους, καὶ τῶν τῆς νεκρότητος ἔργων οὐκ ἀπεσχημένους. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ὧδε ἔχει. {ΚΥΡ.} Τρόπος μὲν γὰρ δὴ πολιτείας τῆς πανάγνου καὶ ἐξῃρημένης οὑτοσὶ, κατὰ τὸν νόμον, μᾶλλον δὲ ὡς ἐν πνεύματί τε καὶ ἀληθείᾳ· σκιὰ γὰρ ὁ νόμος. Ἀλλ' εἰ γένοιτο, φησὶν, ἐπὶ νεκρῷ καταμιανθῆναί ποτε τὸν ἡγιασμένον, ἀποκειρέσθω δή ποτε, καὶ ψιλούσθω τὴν κεφαλὴν, ἀνίερον ἔχων ἤδη πως τὴν κόμην. Καὶ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ὀγδόῃ οἴσει ζεῦγος τρυγόνων, ἢ δύο νεοσσοὺς περιστερῶν. Προσκομιζέτω δὲ, φησὶ, καὶ ἀμνὸν ἐνιαύσιον· καὶ αἱ ἡμέραι αἱ πρῶται ἄλογοι ἔσονται, ὅτι ἐμιάνθη ἡ κεφαλὴ εὐχῆς αὐτοῦ. Εἰ γὰρ γένοιτο τὸν ἡγιασμένον καταῤῥᾳθυμῆσαι τοῦ πρέποντος, καὶ τοῖς εἰς νεκρότητα καταμιανθῆναι τρόποις, ἀπονενευκότα πρὸς τὰ σαρκὸς, ἕψεταί που πάντως αὐτῷ τὸ ἀπεμπωλῆσαι δεῖν τῆς πανάγνου πολιτείας τὰ αὐχήματα, καὶ ἀτιμοτάτην ὥσπερ ἐργάσεται τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κεφαλήν. Ὑπαινίττεται γάρ τι τοιοῦτον ἡ ξύρησις. Εἰκῆ δὲ πεπονηκὼς τὸν παρῳχηκότα χρόνον, τὴν τῶν ἱδρώτων θρηνήσει ζημίαν. Τοῦτο γὰρ, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ, Αἱ ἡμέραι αἱ πρῶται ἄλογοι ἔσονται. Τοιοῦτόν τί φησι καὶ διὰ φωνῆς Ἐζεχιήλ· «Δικαιοσύνη δικαίου οὐ μὴ ἐξέληται αὐτὸν, ἐν ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἁμάρτῃ, καὶ ἀνομία ἀνόμου οὐ μὴ κακώσει αὐτὸν, ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ ἀποστρέψῃ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνομίας αὐτοῦ.» Οὐκοῦν εἰ γένοιτο μεταξὺ καταμιαίνεσθαί πως τοὺς ἡγιασμένους, ζημίαν μὲν ὑποστήσονται τῶν ἤδη προειργασμένων, οὐ μὴν δυσδιάφυκτον τὴν ἐντεῦθεν νοσοῦσι ζημίαν· διασμήχονται γὰρ ἐν Χριστῷ, καθάπερ ἐν τάξει τρυγόνος καὶ περιστερᾶς, ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσάγοντος τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ, καὶ ὡς ἀμνοῦ καταθυομένου, καὶ δικαιοῦντος ἡμᾶς τῷ θανάτῳ τῆς ἰδίας σαρκός. Ταύτῃτοι προστέταχε, τὸν τὴν ξύρησιν ὑπομείναντα θυσίας προσάγειν ἐν τύπῳ Χριστοῦ, τοῦ δικαιοῦντος τὸν ἀσεβῆ, καὶ ῥωννύντος τὸ ἀσθενὲς, καὶ ἀνιστάντος τὸ πεπτωκὸς, καὶ ἐπιστρέφοντος τὸ πλανώμενον, καὶ ἀπονίζοντος τὸ μεμολυσμένον. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἄριστα ἔφης. {ΚΥΡ.} Οἶμαι δ' ἔγωγε, μικρὸν ἐνιέντας τοῖς προκειμένοις τὸν νοῦν, καὶ ἕτερον ἡμᾶς δύνασθαι καταθρῆσαι βάθος λεπτῶν τε καὶ κεκρυμμένων ἐννοιῶν. Παραθήγει γὰρ εἴς γε δὴ τοῦτο ἡμᾶς οὐκ ἀπερισκέπτως ὁ νόμος, περὶ τοῦ τὴν τρίχα τρέφοντος Θεῷ· «Ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ἐξάπινα, παραχρῆμα μιανθήσεται ἡ κεφαλὴ εὐχῆς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ξυρήσεται τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ, ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ καθαρισθῇ, τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ξυρηθήσεται, καὶ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ὀγδόῃ οἴσει δύο τρυγόνας, ἢ δύο νεοσσοὺς περιστερῶν, πρὸς τὸν ἱερέα. Καὶ ἁγιάσει, φησὶ, τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐκείνῃ ἡμέρᾳ.» Προσάγειν δὲ καὶ ἐνιαύσιον ἀμνὸν ἐπετάττετο. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἐπαπορήσειε δ' ἂν εἰκότως ὁ χριστομαθὴς, τί δ' ἂν εἴη λοιπὸν τὸ αἴνιγμα· καὶ πρὸς τί βλέπει μαθητιῶντι φράσον.
pass_a_gloss: CYR. [cont.]: ...among disciples (μαθηταί), saying: [Matthew 8:21–22] Lord, permit (ἐπιτρέπω) me first to go away and bury my father. He: follow me, and let (ἀφίημι) the dead bury their own dead; dead, I think, saying those who chose (αἱρέομαι) to mind (φρονέω) the things in the world (κόσμος) and have not held off (ἀπέχομαι) from works of deadness (νεκρότης). PALL.: Thus it is. CYR.: This is a manner (τρόπος) of all-pure (πάναγνος) and exceptional (ἐξῃρημένη) citizenship (πολιτεία), according to the law, rather as in spirit and truth (ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ); for the law is a shadow (σκιά). But if it happen, he says, that the sanctified one (ἡγιασμένος) be defiled (καταμιαίνομαι) over a dead one, let him be shorn (ἀποκείρομαι) and stripped (ψιλόομαι) on the head, already having the hair unholy (ἀνίερος). On the eighth day he will bring a yoke (ζεῦγος) of turtledoves or two young of doves. Let him bring also a yearling lamb; the first days shall be without account (ἄλογοι), because the head of his vow was defiled. For if the sanctified one should be slack (καταρρᾳθυμέω) about what is fitting, and be defiled by ways (τρόποι) toward deadness, having inclined away (ἀπονεύω) to the things of flesh (σάρξ), it will surely follow him to need to sell away (ἀπεμπολάω) the boasts (αὐχήματα) of the all-pure citizenship, and he will make his own head as it were most dishonored. For the shaving hints (ὑπαινίττομαι) something such. Having toiled (πονέω) in vain (εἰκῇ) the past time, he will lament (θρηνέω) the loss (ζημία) of sweats (ἱδρῶτες). This is: the first days shall be without account. Such he says through Ezekiel's voice: [Ezekiel 33:12] righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) of the righteous shall not deliver (ἐξαιρέομαι) him in the day he sins; lawlessness (ἀνομία) of the lawless shall not harm (κακόω) him in the day he turns back (ἀποστρέφω) from his lawlessness. So if in between (μεταξύ) the sanctified be somehow defiled, they will undergo loss of things already worked (προεργάζομαι), yet they are not sick with (νοσέω) a loss from this hard to escape (δυσδιάφυκτος); for they are scoured clean (διασμήχομαι) in Christ, as in the rank (τάξις) of turtledove and dove, offering (προσάγω) himself for us to the God and Father, and as a lamb being sacrificed (καταθύω), and justifying (δικαιόω) us by the death of his own flesh. Therefore he has ordered (προστάσσω, perf.) the one who endured the shaving to offer sacrifices in type (τύπος) of Christ, who justifies the ungodly (ἀσεβής) [Romans 4:5], and strengthens (ῥώννυμι) the weak, and raises (ἀνίστημι) the fallen, and turns back (ἐπιστρέφω) the wandering (πλανώμενον) [Ezekiel 34:16], and washes off (ἀπονίζω) the stained (μολύνω). PALL.: Best said. CYR.: I think, letting the mind a little into the matters set before us, we can view another depth (βάθος) of fine (λεπτός) and hidden (κρύπτω) thoughts (ἔννοιαι). For the law not without forethought (ἀπερισκέπτως with neg.) sharpens (παραθήγω) us to this, about the one nourishing hair for God: [Numbers 6:9–11] if [one] die suddenly, at once the head of his vow will be defiled, and he will shave his head on the day he is cleansed, on the seventh day; on the eighth day he will bring two turtledoves or two young of doves to the priest; and he will sanctify, it says, his head on that day. And he was ordered to bring a yearling lamb [Numbers 6:12]. PALL.: One taught by Christ (χριστομαθής) might reasonably be at a loss (ἐπαπορέω) what then the riddle (αἴνιγμα) would be; and to what it looks, tell (φράζω) one eager to learn (μαθητιάω).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …among the disciples, saying: ‘Lord, let me first go and bury my father.’ But he said, ‘Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead’ (Matthew 8:21–22). By ‘the dead’, I think, he means those who have chosen to set their minds on the things of the world and have not kept away from the deeds of death.

Cyril: This, then, is the manner of the wholly pure and exceptional way of life according to the law, or rather as it is in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24); for the law is a shadow (Hebrews 10:1). But if it should happen, it says, that the consecrated person is ever defiled over a dead body, let him then be shorn and have his head stripped bare, since his hair has now in a way become unholy. And on the eighth day he shall bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. And let him also bring, it says, a year-old lamb; and the first days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled (Numbers 6:9–12). For if the consecrated person should grow careless of what is fitting and be defiled by ways that lead to deadness, having turned aside to the things of the flesh, it will surely follow that he must barter away the glories of the wholly pure way of life, and he will make his own head, as it were, utterly dishonored. For the shaving hints at something of this kind. And having labored in vain through the time that is past, he will lament the loss of his sweat. This, I think, is the meaning of ‘The first days shall not count.’ He says something like this through the voice of Ezekiel too: ‘The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on the day he sins; and the lawlessness of the lawless shall not harm him on the day he turns from his lawlessness’ (Ezekiel 33:12). So if the consecrated should somehow be defiled in the meantime, they will suffer the loss of what they had already achieved; yet the loss they suffer from it is not hard to escape. For they are scoured clean in Christ, who, in the place, as it were, of the turtledove and the dove, offers himself for us to God the Father, and is sacrificed as a lamb, and justifies us by the death of his own flesh. That is why the law has ordered that the one who has undergone the shaving should offer sacrifices as a type of Christ, who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), strengthens what is weak, raises what has fallen, turns back what has strayed (Ezekiel 34:16), and washes clean what has been stained.

Cyril: But I think that if we apply our minds a little to what lies before us, we can see another depth of subtle and hidden ideas. For the law, not without forethought, spurs us toward this very thing when it speaks of the one who grows his hair for God: ‘But if one dies suddenly, at once the head of his vow shall be defiled; and he shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day he shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest. And he shall sanctify,’ it says, ‘his head on that day’ (Numbers 6:9–11). He was also commanded to offer a year-old lamb (Numbers 6:12).
Palladius: One taught by Christ might well be at a loss to know what, then, the riddle means. I am eager to learn: tell me what it points to.

Opens by continuing the sentence from §20 ('one of those already counted among the disciples'). Matthew 8:21–22 verified (ἐπίτρεψόν μοι πρῶτον ἀπελθεῖν καὶ θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου); the parallel is Luke 9:59–60, but the wording is Matthew's. 'In spirit and truth' alludes to John 4:23–24, the phrase in the title of the work; lowercase 'spirit' follows the majority use in the other Books. 'σκιὰ γὰρ ὁ νόμος' follows Hebrews 10:1 (also compare Colossians 2:17). The Numbers 6:9–12 paraphrase in the first long turn is Cyril's own summary; 'ἄλογοι' rendered 'shall not count'. Ezekiel 33:12 LXX verified; Cyril has 'ἐν ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἁμάρτῃ' where the LXX has 'πλανηθῇ' (compare Ezekiel 18:24–27). 'δικαιοῦντος τὸν ἀσεβῆ' is Romans 4:5 word for word. 'ἐπιστρέφοντος τὸ πλανώμενον' matches Ezekiel 34:16 LXX (τὸ πλανώμενον ἐπιστρέψω), and 'strengthens what is weak' echoes Ezekiel 34:4/16 more loosely; one citation is placed after the shepherd series. 'Offers himself for us to God the Father' may echo Ephesians 5:2 or Hebrews 9:14; left uncited as doubtful. 'Works of deadness' (νεκρότητος ἔργα) may echo Hebrews 6:1 and 9:14 ('dead works'); left uncited. 'προστέταχε' has no expressed subject; English gives 'the law', which is the subject of the next commands. In the final quotation the Greek 'Ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ἐξάπινα' has no 'τις'; rendered 'if one dies' to keep the subject open, since the riddle Palladius asks about turns on it.
